idiom_name: criticality-ranked degraded modes behind a failure detector, with a marked substitute
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: split each function into an essential part and a droppable part, and route every dependency call through one place that (1) detects failure or saturation, (2) tries the primary realization under a bound (timeout, queue limit), and (3) on failure produces the declared substitute and marks the answer as degraded. Keep the ranking - what may be dropped - in configuration or a policy object rather than inside the call sites, so the ladder can be reviewed and changed without touching business code. Degrade per dependency and per criticality, never with one global flag, and switch back to full behaviour automatically once the detector clears - with every transition logged. A useful extension is a monotonic degradation ladder: Level 0 healthy (full functionality), Level 1 degraded (cached or stale data), Level 2 limited (non-critical features disabled), Level 3 minimal (read-only), Level 4 static (defaults only), Level 5 unavailable (clear error with Retry-After). The system should progress through levels in order; skipping directly to unavailable indicates a missing fallback layer.
pitfalls: One global degraded flag couples unrelated functions and can oscillate; degrade per dependency and per criticality.
Falling back silently: always attach the degraded marker, the metric and the reason to the substitute.
Substitutes that fabricate data or keep serving a cache past its TTL turn a dependency outage into a correctness incident.

Fallback loops: service A falls back to B, but B also depends on A and is itself degraded - each retry triggers the other, amplifying load. Break the cycle by ensuring fallback chains are acyclic and independently testable.
Hysteresis failure: the breaker trips too eagerly on transient blips or flaps between open/closed, causing oscillation. Require minimum call counts and a sliding window, not raw failure counts.
Degrading security: the fallback skips authorization checks, serves cached responses without revalidating permissions, or disables rate limiting - turning a resilience feature into a vulnerability.
Metric pollution: degraded requests counted as successful in uptime metrics, hiding the fact that users received a worse experience. Track degraded responses as a separate metric dimension.

Shared-fate fallback: a fallback that queries the same unavailable store or runs on the same saturated pool fails with the primary and consumes the capacity needed for recovery; keep substitutes local or isolate their resources.

Authorization-blind cache fallback: serving a stale personalized or tenant-scoped response without identity-keyed storage and a fresh authorization check can leak data; fall back only to authorization-safe content and mark its freshness.

Unbounded fallback amplification: a timeout can trigger retries, then several fallback calls, multiplying load during an outage; cap attempts and deadlines and ensure the fallback never retries the failed primary.
